solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Refusal to compromise, Irene can’t sign anyway (13)

indicatorNotes.anyway: read as 'any way', it lets the letters go in any order at all

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Irene, stubborn to the end, will not sign the agreement on any terms.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'can’t' is ignored; only its letters C, A, N, T count. The surface even acts out the definition: Irene is being intransigent.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: intransigence, from the Spanish for the uncompromising, is exactly an unwillingness to meet anyone halfway.

entries.clue: It’s extremely small and free of charge (7)

annotation.definition: It’s extremely small and free of charge

blocks.note: read as something little and cheap, and meant as something on the subatomic scale
read as costing nothing, and meant as carrying no electric charge

annotation.surface: A bargain: something tiny that costs nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like shopping; it is physics. Charge here is electric, not a price.
annotation.definitionFit: The neutron is the particle in the atomic nucleus with no electric charge, which is where its name comes from: it is neutral.

entries.clue: Travel free over the Orient (4)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down clue the first piece sits physically over the second, so RID goes on top of E

blocks.note: to rid someone of a burden is to free them
the Orient is the East, E

annotation.surface: A cheap trip to the Far East.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Travel free' looks like one phrase about a free trip; the definition is just 'Travel'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to ride is to travel on a horse, bike or bus, and 'ride' as a noun is a journey.

entries.clue: Two-year-olds may run in it — in two ways (7)

annotation.definition: Two-year-olds may run in it — in two ways

blocks.note: read as toddlers tearing about a playroom, and also meant as young racehorses entered for a race
the setter's own signal that both readings are meant, not a separate instruction

annotation.surface: Small children dashing about their playroom.
annotation.walkthrough: A nursery is a room or school for small children, and in racing a nursery is a handicap race for two-year-old horses.
annotation.definitionFit: Toddlers of two run around in a nursery, and two-year-old horses run in a nursery, the racing name for a handicap restricted to their age.

entries.clue: Complaint one’s taken to head about two students (7)

indicatorNotes.taken to: I is taken along and attached at the front of what follows
indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in the sense of 'around, near': LL is placed next to NESS

blocks.note: one = I, the Roman numeral
L = learner, a student, twice
a ness is a headland, as in Sheerness or Dungeness

annotation.surface: Someone taking a grievance to the headteacher about a couple of pupils.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' sounds like a grievance and 'head' like a headteacher; both are misdirection. NESS is a head in the coastal sense, a promontory.
annotation.definitionFit: A second sense: 'complaint' is also a medical word for an ailment, as in 'a stomach complaint'.

entries.clue: Snick a boundary? (4)

blocks.note: in cricket, a snick is a thin deflection off the side of the bat
a border or limit, the rim of something

annotation.surface: A cricketer nicking the ball away for four.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket a boundary is a hit that reaches the rope, which makes the question mark tease; here it simply means a border.
annotation.definitionFit: A batsman who snicks the ball gets an edge on it, and the edge of a field or table is its boundary.

entries.clue: Entry of animal makes Tom panic (7)

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
in a flap = in a panic

annotation.surface: A beast bursting in and sending someone called Tom into a panic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a man's name; it is the tomcat.
annotation.definitionFit: Described by its use: a cat flap is the small hinged door by which a pet cat comes into the house.

entries.clue: Soldier escort arranged for individually-owned businesses (7,6)

indicatorNotes.arranged: to arrange is to put in order, so ESCORT's letters are set out in a new one

blocks.note: a private is a soldier of the lowest rank
anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: A military escort laid on for some private companies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soldier escort' reads as one military phrase; the words split into a soldier and some letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: The economic term: the private sector is the part of the economy owned by individuals and companies, as against the state-run public sector.

entries.clue: You may get a ring back to confirm this (6,7)

annotation.definition: You may get a ring back to confirm this

blocks.clueFragment: You may get a ring back
blocks.note: read as a returned phone call, and meant as an engagement ring handed back
read as confirming an arrangement, and meant as the proof that the engagement is off

annotation.surface: Someone calling back on the phone to confirm an arrangement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring back' is the phone phrase for returning a call; the ring here is the one on a finger.
annotation.definitionFit: When an engagement is broken off, the ring is traditionally returned, so getting it back confirms the romance is over.

entries.clue: Nearer the circle, or back beneath (7)

indicatorNotes.back: 'back' as in going back the way you came, so OR is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: the word 'or' taken as letters and turned round
beneath = under

annotation.surface: Theatre seating: nearer the dress circle, or down at the back of the stalls.
annotation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a joining word offering an alternative; it is letters for the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A comparative: a shape that is rounder is closer to being a perfect circle.

entries.clue: The girl turns out as substitute for the match (7)

indicatorNotes.turns out: to turn out something is to empty and rearrange it, so THE GIRL's letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A girl brought on as a reserve player for a big game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Substitute' and 'match' suggest a team game; the match is the one you strike.
annotation.definitionFit: Described by use: a cigarette lighter makes a flame and so does the job you would otherwise strike a match for.

entries.clue: Girl getting rave review (4)

indicatorNotes.review: to review is to go over again, and the letters of RAVE are gone over into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 4 letters

annotation.surface: A young woman receiving glowing notices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rave review' is a stock phrase for high praise; here it splits into fodder and instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword convention: 'girl' stands for any girl's name, and Vera is one.

entries.clue: Put off Edward’s return with hesitation (5)

indicatorNotes.return: to return is to come back, so TED is read backwards

blocks.note: Ted, short for Edward, turned round
er, the sound of hesitating

annotation.surface: Edward postponing his homecoming after some dithering.
annotation.walkthrough: Edward must first become its nickname TED before it is turned round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to deter someone is to discourage them from acting, to put them off.

entries.clue: Criticism that’s directed at flying machines? (4)

blocks.note: a barrage of hostile comment
anti-aircraft fire, from the German Fliegerabwehrkanone

annotation.surface: Hostile comments aimed at aircraft designers.
annotation.walkthrough: The figurative sense came from the literal one: taking flak was first what bomber crews did.
annotation.definitionFit: Flak was wartime anti-aircraft fire, and its image of a barrage gave the everyday sense of heavy criticism.

entries.clue: Inclined to get slim before beginning to tan (5)

indicatorNotes.before: 'before' in the sense of 'ahead of in order', so LEAN comes first and T follows
indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so take the first letter of 'tan'

blocks.note: slim = lean
first letter of tan

annotation.surface: Someone keen to slim down before starting on a suntan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inclined to' reads as 'keen to'; the definition is 'Inclined' in the sense of tilted.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are past tenses of a tilt: a ladder that has leant against a wall is inclined against it.

entries.clue: Fast? Nothing! It’s slow (5)

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
nothing = O, zero

annotation.surface: Mocking something supposedly fast as not fast at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast' opposes 'slow' in the surface, but it means going without food; the question mark flags Lent as an example of a fast.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical term: lento, Italian for slow, is the tempo marking for a slow passage.

entries.clue: Girl brought in to have a go at leather-making (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a tannery is the place where leather-making happens

indicatorNotes.brought in to: something brought in to a place ends up inside it, so ANNE goes inside TRY

blocks.note: to have a go = to try
a girl's name

annotation.surface: A young woman taken on to try her hand at working leather.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads straight on to 'at', which only joins it to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Named by its trade: a tannery is the works where hides are tanned, the main step in leather-making.

entries.clue: New taps fitted as kitchen equipment (7)

indicatorNotes.fitted: pieces that are fitted are put together into a new shape, and so are these letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A plumber installing new taps in a fitted kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like the anagram signal; it is part of the fodder, and 'fitted' does the work.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a stewpan, a deep lidded pan for slow cooking, is one item of kitchen equipment.

entries.clue: Supports inferior goods (7)

blocks.note: a verb: backs a motion or proposal
a noun: slightly flawed items sold off cheap

annotation.surface: Someone backing cheap, substandard merchandise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supports' looks like a noun, props or braces; it is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: At a meeting whoever seconds a motion supports it, and factory seconds are goods not good enough to sell at full price.

entries.clue: Be fond of nurse (4,3)

blocks.note: to feel affection for
a verb: to look after someone ill

annotation.surface: Having a soft spot for a nurse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nurse' looks like a noun; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase carries both senses: 'I care for her' can mean I love her or I look after her.

entries.clue: Hanger-on holding money for a Scotsman (7)

annotation.definition: Hanger-on holding money for a Scotsman

blocks.note: read as a sponger, and meant literally as something that hangs on the front of a kilt
read as looking after a Scot's cash, and meant as a purse, since a kilt has no pockets

annotation.surface: A parasitic hanger-on keeping a Scot's cash.
annotation.walkthrough: A hanger-on is normally a person; here it is a thing that hangs.
annotation.definitionFit: The sporran is the pouch worn hanging from the belt of a kilt, doing the job of the pockets a kilt lacks.

entries.clue: Firm follows new trade in old-fashioned style (3,4)

indicatorNotes.follows: one thing that follows another comes after it, so CO goes at the end
indicatorNotes.new: 'new' in the sense of made over, so TRADE's letters take a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters
Co. = company, a firm

annotation.surface: A company moving into a new line of business with a retro look.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective, solid; it is a company.
annotation.definitionFit: A period style: Art Deco, the bold geometric design of the 1920s and 30s, now reads as vintage.

entries.clue: A London club magazine (7)

blocks.note: the north London football club
a store of arms and ammunition

annotation.surface: A members' club in London with its own publication.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Magazine' suggests a publication; it is a weapons store.
annotation.definitionFit: Arsenal is a London football club named after the Woolwich arsenal, and an arsenal, like a magazine, is where munitions are kept.

entries.clue: Converted highest fractions (7)

indicatorNotes.Converted: something converted is changed into a new form, and HIGHEST's letters are changed into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: Top-scoring fractions after a conversion in maths.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is maths homework, which keeps 'Converted' looking like arithmetic rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: an eighth is one of the fractions, one part in eight.

entries.clue: A bit of a wag, even a joker maybe (4)

blocks.note: an amusing, eccentric person
the joker is one member of a pack, hence 'maybe' marking an example

annotation.surface: Describing someone as something of a comedian.
annotation.walkthrough: The two definitions look like one idea said twice; the second 'joker' is the playing card.
annotation.definitionFit: Calling someone 'a real card' means they are a wag, and a joker is an example of a playing card.

entries.clue: Heroin that’s found in the gym? (5)

blocks.note: slang for the drug
the padded box gymnasts vault over, a piece of gym apparatus

annotation.surface: Drugs turning up in a gymnasium.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a doping scandal; the gym item is the box you vault over.
annotation.definitionFit: Horse is old street slang for heroin, and the horse is the padded apparatus gymnasts vault over.

entries.clue: Enthralled by India, gracious setting for a famous sight (4)

indicatorNotes.Enthralled by: someone enthralled is held captive, and the answer is held captive inside these words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'India' across the comma into 'gracious'

annotation.surface: A visitor captivated by India's charm and one of its great monuments.
annotation.walkthrough: The hidden word straddles the comma: indiA GRAcious. The famous sight is the Taj Mahal.
annotation.definitionFit: Agra is the Indian city on the Yamuna where the Taj Mahal stands, so it is the setting for the famous sight.

entries.clue: The lowest sort of people, that one always finds at the top (4)

annotation.definition2: that one always finds at the top

blocks.note: a term of contempt for the worst of society

blocks.clueFragment: that one always finds at the top
blocks.note: literally, the film that rises to the surface of a liquid

annotation.surface: A cynic's remark that the worst people always rise to the top.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is the contradiction: the lowest thing is always found at the top.
annotation.definitionFit: Scum is contemptuous slang for the vilest people, and literally the froth that floats on top of a pond or pan.

entries.clue: Stone work which is above a learner (4)

indicatorNotes.which is above: in a down clue the first piece sits physically above the next, so OP goes over A and L

blocks.note: op. = opus, a work
used as is
L for learner, as on L-plates

annotation.surface: Masonry work that is too hard for a beginner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stone work' reads as masonry; the definition is 'Stone' alone.
annotation.definitionFit: In the sense of gemstone: the opal is a precious stone known for its shifting colours.

entries.clue: Position right for military leader (7)

blocks.note: an office is a post, a position
R = right

annotation.surface: The correct job for a commander.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Position right' reads as 'the correct post'; the words work separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an officer is anyone holding a commission, who leads troops in the armed forces.

entries.clue: Relatively favourable (7)

blocks.note: read as 'fairly, comparatively', and meant as 'towards relatives'
read as 'positive', and meant as 'showing favour'

annotation.surface: Something described as fairly positive.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is a pun on 'relatively': it describes favouring your relatives.
annotation.definitionFit: Nepotic is the adjective from nepotism, the favouring of relatives when handing out jobs.

entries.clue: Fagin’s pupils were members of it (8,5)

annotation.definition: Fagin’s pupils were members of it

blocks.note: Fagin in Dickens's Oliver Twist trains boys as pickpockets, so his pupils are young thieves
read as belonging to a school class, and meant as belonging to a social class

annotation.surface: A school register for Fagin's young pupils.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' and 'class' suggest a schoolroom; the class is a social one, the Victorian phrase for the underworld.
annotation.definitionFit: The criminal class was the Victorian term for the underworld, and Fagin's pickpockets were both in it and a class of his pupils.
